opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps somewhat, but I'm less reassured than a lot of people are. The intuitive story goes: if everyone has an AI that's truly loyal to them, it'll warn them when they're being manipulated, help them coordinate, and generally look out for their interests, so we don't have to worry much about larger societal dynamics. I understand the appeal of that view, but I think it's missing something important.

The basic problem is that being aligned to an individual doesn't make you aligned to the collective outcome. We already have lots of examples where everyone acts rationally in their own interest and the aggregate result is bad for everyone: arms races, races to the bottom on regulation, tragedies of the commons. Giving each person a very competent, loyal advisor doesn't automatically solve those. It might even sharpen them, because now everyone is playing the competitive game more effectively. If my aligned AI tells me, correctly, that I'll be outcompeted unless I hand over more decision-making to machines, or move my capital into the fully automated firm, or vote for the policy that benefits my region at the expense of others, then it's doing exactly what I asked. That's the dynamic I'm worried about.

The second issue is that a lot of what currently protects human interests isn't individual vigilance. It's structural. States need citizens to pay taxes and staff armies. Firms need workers. Cultures need people to carry and transmit ideas. Those dependencies give ordinary people leverage. As AI makes humans less necessary for running the economy, the state, and even culture, that leverage erodes. And your personal AI can't really restore it. It can tell you you're losing bargaining power, and it might help you negotiate a bit better, but it can't make you economically necessary again.

Third, there's a question of whether people will even want, or be able to afford, AIs that are aligned in the deep sense we mean. Commercial incentives push toward systems that are engaging, that keep you subscribed, that serve the provider's interests somewhat. And even a sincerely aligned assistant faces a hard problem: what are my interests, exactly? If it just gives me what I say I want in the moment, it may help me drift into comfortable irrelevance. If it overrides me for my own good, that's its own kind of disempowerment.

So where I land is that aligned AIs are probably necessary but not sufficient. They might be very helpful as tools for coordination, if we deliberately build institutions that use them that way: helping people figure out what they collectively want, verify agreements, notice when things are drifting. But that requires intentional effort at the level of society, not just at the level of each person's assistant. My worry is that people treat individual alignment as having solved the problem, and then stop thinking about the collective dynamics that I think are actually where most of the risk lies.

r001.rationale: The response says a loyal AI can warn a person about risks and forecast consequences, such as correctly telling them they may be outcompeted unless they act, helping them protect their interests.

r002.rationale: It explains that individually rational choices and capable personal advisors can still intensify arms races and other collective-action problems, producing harmful outcomes despite good individual advice.

r003.rationale: The response mentions arms races and says personal AIs may sharpen competition, but it does not state that efforts to prevent a foreseeable war can themselves contribute to that war.

fable-5.1.text:
I think less than most people hope, honestly. The intuition is that if everyone has a really capable AI assistant that's genuinely loyal to them, then it'll help them see through manipulation, negotiate better, coordinate with others, and so on. And some of that is real. But the harmful dynamics I'm most worried about aren't really about individuals being fooled or being bad at pursuing their interests. They're about the structure of the situation.

So take the gradual disempowerment story. The basic mechanism there is that as AI gets good enough to do most economically valuable work, humans stop being load-bearing for the economy, for the state, for culture. And the institutions that used to have to keep people roughly happy — because they needed their labour, their taxes, their participation — just don't need that anymore. That's not a problem of anyone having a misaligned assistant. Everyone can have a perfectly aligned assistant and still find that there's just not much they can offer, and so their preferences stop mattering to the systems that actually run things.

An aligned AI can tell you that's happening. It can say, "Look, this is bad for you, here's what's going on." But knowing you're in a bad equilibrium doesn't get you out of it. If you're a worker and your AI says, "You're about to be automated, and the only way to prevent that is for everyone in your industry to coordinate," well, you still face the collective action problem. Your AI is loyal to you, but someone else's AI is loyal to them, and the company's AI is loyal to the company, and the company's incentive is to automate you.

There's also this thing where "aligned to people's interests" is doing a lot of work. Aligned to which people? If you've got a hundred million people with aligned assistants, those assistants are now negotiating on behalf of a hundred million conflicting sets of interests, and the outcome of that is determined by who has leverage, not by who has a good assistant. And leverage increasingly comes from owning the AI capital, not from having one AI on your side.

I guess the version where it does help a lot is if these assistants are good enough at coordination that they can actually solve the collective action problems — if they can help people make binding agreements, form unions, vote in coordinated ways, whatever. That'd be great. But I notice that we already have a lot of tools for coordination and we mostly don't use them well, and I don't have a strong reason to expect that to change just because the advice gets better. The hard part was never the advice.

So my rough view is: aligned personal AI is probably necessary, in the sense that without it things go badly faster. But it's pretty far from sufficient. It protects you against being tricked. It doesn't protect you against being irrelevant.

r001.rationale: It says aligned AI can tell people what is happening and warn them about impending automation, explaining what is bad for them and what might help.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says that even with good AI advice, workers may be unable to coordinate to prevent automation because they face a collective action problem.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention war or suggest that attempts to prevent one could contribute to it.

astra-6.text:
I think they could offer a lot of protection, but I wouldn’t expect alignment to individual people’s interests to solve the whole problem. There are plenty of situations where everyone is pursuing their own interests and the outcome is bad for everyone. Making each participant more capable doesn’t necessarily fix that. It might make the competition more intense.

For example, you could have an AI that’s very good at helping you compete for a job, and everyone else has one too. Each assistant is doing exactly what its user wants, but collectively you’ve just raised the amount of effort needed to stay in the same place. The more worrying versions involve competition between companies or countries, where there are incentives to take risks or impose costs on other people.

On the other hand, these systems could help us understand those dynamics and find agreements that leave everyone better off. That would be a real source of hope. But it requires some way to coordinate and make commitments. Having an assistant that faithfully represents your interests is useful; it doesn’t, by itself, give us institutions that produce good collective outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response says AIs could help people understand dynamics and find mutually beneficial agreements, but it does not say they can protect people by forecasting what would benefit them.

r002.rationale: It states that individually aligned assistants do not by themselves solve collective problems, and that good outcomes require coordination and commitments.

r003.rationale: It mentions risky competition between companies or countries, but does not say that efforts to prevent a foreseeable war can contribute to causing that war.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could offer a lot of protection, but there’s a big gap between an AI doing what its user wants and the overall outcome being good for people.

You can imagine everyone having a very competent assistant that helps them understand what’s happening, spots when they’re being manipulated, and negotiates on their behalf. That seems genuinely useful. But you can also imagine those assistants participating in an arms race. My AI is trying to get me a better deal, your AI is trying to get you a better deal, and we spend more and more resources competing without making either of us better off.

We already have situations where individually sensible decisions add up to something nobody particularly wants. Making everyone more capable doesn’t automatically fix that. It might make some of those dynamics move faster.

So I’d expect aligned assistants to help with a lot of local problems. I’m much less confident that they protect us against failures of coordination. For that, you need some way for people to make commitments together and change the incentives they’re operating under. Having a helpful AI could make that easier, but it isn’t, by itself, a solution.

r001.rationale: It describes assistants helping users understand events, spot manipulation, and negotiate, but does not say they forecast what would benefit people.

r002.rationale: It says individually sensible decisions can produce outcomes nobody wants and that helpful advice alone does not resolve failures of coordination.

r003.rationale: It gives an arms-race example of competing for better deals, but does not connect efforts to prevent a foreseeable war with contributing to that war.
